item.title: When treatments create new conditions | Science
item.description: When the actor Sam Neill died unexpectedly in July this year, media reports emphasized that his death was not due to cancer. Neill was diagnosed in 2022 with angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma, a form of blood cancer commonly treated with chemotherapy combining as many as five different anticancer drugs. Although initially successful, after four years in remission he stopped responding to chemotherapy. At that point he entered a clinical trial testing the effectiveness of CAR (chimaeric antigen receptor) T-cell therapy in this type of cancer. In CAR T-cell therapies, which have been approved for blood cancers, the patient’s own T cells are genetically modified to recognize and destroy the cancer cells in their body. Neill seems to have responded well, and in April 2026 he publicly announced that he was “cancer-free.” Yet only four months later he was dead, and many people were puzzled about what had “gone wrong.”

item.title: Protect the Third Pole from mineral mining | Science
item.description: The global green-energy transition has led to soaring demand for critical minerals (1), placing unprecedented extraction pressure on fragile alpine ecosystems such as the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau (QTP), also known as the Third Pole, which hosts more than 3000 valuable mineral deposits (2). Most active mines in the QTP are located at altitudes exceeding 4000 m (3, 4), wheremining activities could accelerate permafrost thaw and pollute water (4) on which millions of downstream residents depend (5). On 15 May, China’s State Council passed regulations requiring local governments to investigate and assess ecological damage and environmental pollution caused by mining activities (6). Local governments in the QTP should adhere to the law by strengthening supervision and ecosystem management of mining activities.

item.title: Combat Galapagos marine iguana trafficking | Science
item.description: On 28 August, 32 Galapagos marine iguanas (Amblyrhynchus cristatus) were confiscated in Ecuador’s Quito airport from a passenger bound for Iceland (1). Similar seizures took place in May, when 12 live marine iguanas were found at Guayaquil’s airport (2) and four more were rescued from a residential area (1, 2). These reptiles, highly desired by exotic pet collectors, are endemic to the Galapagos Islands and classified as Vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (3). Ecuadorian law prohibits their removal (4), and the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) prohibits their international trade (5). The recent smuggling attempts reveal that Ecuador’s wildlife-detection control measures, such as x-ray baggage scanners (6, 7), are insufficient (2, 6). To protect marine iguanas, Ecuador must address the gaps in its wildlife trafficking policies.
